papers.title: RECONFIGURABLE ROBOTIC SWARMS AND CONTINUOUS FUNCTIONAL REGENERATION AT THE LIMIT STARLI Research Works | White Rainbow Scientific Library | Flagship 02 Prospective Research Atlas — English Review Edition, October 2026 Can a distributed population of heterogeneous modular robots reconstruct an operationally qualified capability after damage, without treating a newly assembled shape as evidence of restored function? Reconfigurable Robotic Swarms and Continuous Functional Regeneration at the Limit develops an interdisciplinary research program on modular morphology, distributed self-assembly, task-dependent graph structure, mechanical qualification, connector fatigue, recoverable actions, and independent post-reconfiguration verification. Its central proposition is deliberately testable: a swarm may change its topology after losing modules, but it earns the stronger name of functional regeneration only when its restored configuration satisfies the original, independently assessed service requirements and does not conceal emerging hazards or latent joint failures. The monograph distinguishes three often conflated networks: mechanical connections that transmit forces, communication links that transmit information, and power connections that transport energy. It then investigates how graph connectivity, geometric rigidity, elastic stiffness, buckling, frictional contact, thermal dissipation, material fatigue, sensing uncertainty, local negotiation, and safe rollback constrain what an apparently repaired swarm can actually do. A prospective twenty-module testbed provides recurring engineering anchors: bridge, gripping, and sensing-tower tasks, blinded removal of modules, unseen configurations, independent qualification, and strong comparisons with redundant fixed structures and specialist replacement procedures. The research architecture includes thirty mathematically diverse derivation plates, eighty-two chapter-level questions and their five individually paginated study units, two hundred falsifiable Research Gates, and thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos. The companion spreadsheet links physical models, chapter topics, prospective study cards, provenance, source DOI records, and page references to support future research and AI-assisted scientific handoff. Published robotics literature supplies a source-grounded context for modular reconfigurable mechanisms and fault-aware planning, including external DOI records for reviews and an existing fault-tolerant modular system. The manuscript separates those precedents from its own unexecuted research designs. Its two STARLI mother volumes are listed as conceptual ancestry, not as independent experimental validation. Biological regeneration functions as an analogy for staged assessment of restoration, not as evidence of biomedical efficacy, autonomous human-tissue repair, or indefinite machine life. This is a prospective research-atlas REVIEW EDITION. The mathematical relations, study proposals, design seeds, and acceptance thresholds are not experimentally validated findings. External mathematical review, whole-text DOI auditing, and a stronger editorial review for chapter-level semantic repetition remain necessary before scholarly publication. Negative findings, conventional method superiority, irreversible module retirement, and scientific abstention are legitimate outcomes within this research program. papers.title: Immune Compatible Biohybrid Swarms and Self Repairing Interfaces at the Limit English Publication Description STARLI Flagship 10 30 Physicalized Models 82 Chapters 200 Research Gates Immune Compatible Biohybrid Swarms and Self Repairing Interfaces at the Limit is a high-density research monograph on living cellular actuators joined to synthetic microrobotic swarms. It asks whether hybrid agents can perform pumping and local repair while preserving cell identity, immune compatibility, material traceability, independent stop authority, and complete terminal disposition. The book distinguishes recovered motion from recovered compatibility. Biological healing can restore contractile force while antigen burden, inflammatory signaling, interface damage, identity drift, or shed material continues to rise. Every started culture and device remains in the evidence denominator, including failed actuators, immune excursions, lost modules, and incomplete retrievals. Thirty physicalized models connect muscle force velocity, calcium excitation, fatigue and recovery, cardiac synchrony, neuromuscular control, optogenetics, metabolism, active traction, interfacial fracture, antigen presentation, complement, protein corona, macrophage states, fibrosis, cytokine feedback, identity drift, clonal safety, mass closure, degradation, retrieval, controllability, residual detection, and lifecycle reliability. Eighty-two chapters develop the research architecture through five one-page sections per chapter. Two hundred Research Gates specify matched pure synthetic and pure biological baselines, blinded challenges, paired measurements, adversarial explanations, and pass, fail, abstain, or domain-restriction outcomes. No gate can pass on restored force alone. The monograph remains within controlled in vitro and compliant pretransplant research. It does not infer clinical safety from movement, short-term viability, low bulk cytokine levels, or apparent disappearance after retrieval. Its Phoenix Answer Embryo, the Biohybrid Interface Passport, binds cell source, material identity, immune history, actuation, drift, shed mass, withdrawal, and residual evidence into one auditable record. This volume is intended for researchers in biohybrid robotics, biomaterials, immunoengineering, tissue engineering, microrobotics, cellular biomechanics, control, metrology, and translational manufacturing. It is designed for successor research: its models and gates can be executed, falsified, narrowed, or extended without inheriting hidden culture or operator assumptions.
